issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s share fixed by a final preliminary decree must be given effect in the final partition proceedings and cannot be reduced by reopening matters already decided.
material_facts: A prior judgment finally declared the plaintiff branch entitled to a fixed share in the joint family properties and defined the properties to be divided.
The current appeals arose from proceedings to work out the final partition.
The defendants argued that the plaintiff branch’s possession of securities and their subsequent unavailability justified denying or reducing its share.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff branch remained entitled to the share declared in the preliminary decree; the final partition proceedings could not reopen that entitlement.
issues.legal_principle: A preliminary decree conclusively declares the parties’ shares and the properties to be divided, and matters decided by it cannot be readjudicated in final-decree proceedings. The Court applied the prior inter partes decision in M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty.

predicates.final_partition_proceeding: The dispute is being determined in proceedings to implement a preliminary decree by making a final partition.
predicates.preliminary_decree_fixed_share: An earlier binding preliminary decree declared a co-sharer’s share in the properties to be partitioned.
predicates.attempted_reopening_of_fixed_share: A party seeks to use the final partition proceedings to revisit or reduce the share already declared.

issues.definition: When final partition proceedings implement a preliminary decree that fixed a co-sharer’s share, an attempt to reopen that share does not prevent its effectuation.

issues.legal_issue: A direction to respect the parties’ existing possession as far as possible does not bar an out-of-possession co-sharer from receiving immovable property in the final partition.
material_facts: The prior decree declared the plaintiff branch’s share and directed that existing possession be respected as far as possible.
The defendants possessed coffee estates and other immovable properties, while the trial court allotted the plaintiff branch securities and bonds based on their values at an earlier date.
The plaintiff branch challenged being denied any share in the immovable properties.
The trial court’s allocation did not provide for equalization of the value of the parties’ shares.
issues.conclusion: The possession direction did not require the plaintiff branch to be excluded from immovable property; possession should be preserved where practicable through value equalization, and partition need not divide every item among all co-sharers.
issues.legal_principle: In partition, the allotment need not give each co-sharer a portion of every item. Properties of unequal value may be allotted to different co-sharers, with adjustments, including payment to equalize values. The direction to respect possession as far as possible does not make possession an absolute bar to allotment. The Court applied the partition procedure in Order 20 Rule 18 and Order 26 Rules 13–14 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: final_partition_proceeding and preliminary_decree_fixed_shares and qualified_direction_to_respect_possession and claimant_out_of_possession_of_immovable_property

predicates.final_partition_proceeding: The dispute is being determined in proceedings to implement a preliminary decree by making a final partition.
predicates.preliminary_decree_fixed_shares: An earlier binding preliminary decree declared the co-sharers’ respective shares in the properties.
predicates.qualified_direction_to_respect_possessio: The decree directs that existing possession be respected only where practicable.
predicates.claimant_out_of_possession_of_immovable_: The co-sharer seeking an allotment does not possess the immovable property held by another co-sharer.

issues.definition: In final partition proceedings with fixed shares and a qualified direction to preserve possession, a co-sharer’s lack of possession does not itself prevent an allotment of immovable property.

issues.legal_issue: The value of property being divided in a partition is ordinarily determined as of the final decree.
material_facts: The suit had been pending for many years between the preliminary decree and the final partition.
The parties disputed the use of an earlier valuation date for allocating the properties.
The Court noted that property values may change substantially during the time taken to complete partition.
issues.conclusion: The valuation for the partition is to be made as of the date of the final decree, subject to adjustments the court considers appropriate to balance the equities where circumstances warrant them.
issues.legal_principle: The actual partition is effected by the final decree, so valuation ordinarily relates to that date. Order 20 Rule 18 and Order 26 Rules 13–14 of the Code of Civil Procedure govern partition and permit the court and commissioner to make the inquiries and adjustments needed to allot shares. The Court distinguished Khatoon Bibi v. Abdul Wahab Sahib, where the circumstances included dissipation of the entire movable property and no property being available for partition.

predicates.final_partition_proceeding: The dispute is being determined in proceedings to implement a preliminary decree by making a final partition.
predicates.property_values_are_used_to_allocate_sha: The properties must be valued to determine what property or adjustment each co-sharer receives.

issues.definition: When property values are used to allocate shares in final partition proceedings, the ordinary valuation date is the date of the final decree.

issues.legal_issue: The unavailability or alleged dissipation of assets previously held by a co-sharer does not by itself extinguish that co-sharer’s share in the joint family properties.
material_facts: The plaintiff branch possessed securities, bonds, and shares at the time identified in the preliminary decree, and those assets were then worth more than its share of the joint properties.
Most of those securities were no longer available.
The defendants alleged that the plaintiff branch had disposed of the assets and sought to rely on their absence to support denying the branch an allotment from the remaining properties.
The preliminary decree had already declared the plaintiff branch’s share.
issues.conclusion: The assets’ non-availability alone did not deprive the plaintiff branch of its declared share. Their value, and any resulting excess for which the branch must account, is to be determined in the partition by reference to the applicable valuation date; the Court expressed no opinion on whether dissipation occurred.
issues.legal_principle: The final partition must give effect to the share declared in the preliminary decree. The absence of assets does not, by itself, justify denying that share; any excess value held or dissipated may instead be brought into account. The Court applied the binding preliminary decree and its rule that partition valuation is ordinarily as of the final decree.

predicates.final_partition_proceeding: The dispute is being determined in proceedings to implement a preliminary decree by making a final partition.
predicates.preliminary_decree_fixed_share: An earlier binding preliminary decree declared a co-sharer’s share in the properties to be partitioned.
predicates.previously_held_partition_assets_unavail: Assets that were held by a co-sharer and were relevant to the partition are no longer available when the final partition is being worked out.

issues.definition: In final partition proceedings, the absence of previously held partition assets alone does not extinguish a share fixed by the preliminary decree.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer in possession of joint family property must account to the other co-sharers for income received from that property from severance of joint status until final partition.
material_facts: The prior decree fixed the date from which the family members held the joint family properties as tenants in common.
The decree required accounting for rents, income, profits, and dividends received from joint family properties in each party’s possession until final partition.
The defendants disputed their obligation to account for income from the joint properties after the date of severance.
issues.conclusion: The parties in possession were liable to account to the others for rents, income, profits, and dividends received from joint family properties from the date of severance until the final decree.
issues.legal_principle: After severance of joint status, the members become tenants in common. A member in possession who receives rents and profits from joint property must account for those receipts to the other co-sharers. The Court applied the binding prior decision in M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty, which relied on John Kennedy v. Mary Annette De Trafford and referred to Gulabrao Fakirrao v. Baburao Fakirrao.

predicates.partition_proceeding_after_severance: The dispute concerns the division of property after the co-owners’ joint status has ended.
predicates.co_sharer_received_income_from_joint_pro: A co-sharer in possession received rent, income, profits, or dividends from property that remained joint property pending partition.

issues.definition: After joint status ends, a co-sharer who receives income from undivided joint property must account for that income to the other co-sharers.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer is not required to account to the other co-sharers for profits or acquisitions from a separate business carried on after severance of joint status.
material_facts: The prior decree established that joint status had severed and that businesses carried on by the parties after severance were separate businesses.

The defendants challenged the direction requiring them to account for income from joint properties, while the earlier binding decision distinguished that income from profits and acquisitions made through separate businesses.
issues.conclusion: The parties were not liable to account to one another for profits earned or acquisitions made in their separate businesses after severance, although they remained liable to account for income received from joint family property.
issues.legal_principle: On severance, members become tenants in common of the family property, but profits and acquisitions from a member’s separate business are not thereby family assets and are not accountable to the other members. The Court applied the binding prior decision in M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty, which relied on John Kennedy v. Mary Annette De Trafford and referred to Gulabrao Fakirrao v. Baburao Fakirrao.

predicates.severance_of_joint_status: The co-owners’ joint status has ended, leaving them as co-owners of the property pending partition.
predicates.co_sharer_earned_profits_or_made_acquisi: After severance, a co-sharer earned profits or acquired property through a business carried on separately from the other co-sharers.

issues.definition: After joint status ends, profits and acquisitions generated by a co-sharer’s separate business are not subject to accounting to the other co-sharers.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer who manages or possesses property for the family is not, merely for that reason, a trustee owing fiduciary duties to the other co-sharers.
material_facts: The defendants argued that the plaintiff branch had held valuable securities as trustee for the family and had breached that trust by disposing of them.
The earlier inter partes decision had rejected the contention that a co-tenant was a trustee of the other co-tenants.
The securities’ unavailability was relied on to support treating their disposition as a breach of trust and denying the plaintiff branch an allotment.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the claim that the plaintiff branch’s status as a co-sharer or its possession of the securities made it a trustee, and that contention did not justify the trial court’s allocation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act was invoked by the defendants, but the Court held that a fiduciary relationship does not arise merely because one tenant in common manages property or another leaves property in that co-tenant’s possession. It relied on John Kennedy v. Mary Annette De Trafford, which had been approved in the prior inter partes decision, M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty.

predicates.co_ownership_of_property: Two or more persons hold undivided interests in the same property.
predicates.possession_or_management_by_one_co_owner: One co-owner possesses or manages the property while the others have interests in it.
predicates.no_independent_basis_for_fiduciary_relat: No circumstance beyond co-ownership and possession or management establishes a separate fiduciary relationship.

issues.definition: When a co-owner merely possesses or manages jointly owned property and there is no independent basis for a fiduciary relationship, co-ownership alone does not make that person a trustee.
